description: We are Team Agastya, a student team passionate about space, engineering and technology. We chose “Flame in Freefall” because fire behaves differently in microgravity, making combustion important for spacecraft safety. We want to explore NASA’s open data and build an AI-powered tool to make complex research easier to understand and uncover useful fire-safety insights.
summary:
FLAMORA – Flame in Free Fall

Team: Agastya

FLAMORA transforms NASA's microgravity fire experiments into an interactive platform for exploring space combustion research.

We collected and organised 1,825 test records from 23 NASA investigations, including BASS, FLEX, Saffire and ACME. The platform features a Research Hub to explore NASA datasets, visualise real experimental measurements and compare investigations.

Its AI Research Assistant answers questions using cited NASA sources and supports multilingual interaction and voice input. The Mission Brief feature identifies experiments relevant to different space environments, including the ISS, Moon and Mars, while highlighting existing research gaps.

The Fire Simulation Lab allows users to explore how gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure and airflow affect flame behaviour. Simulated results are clearly distinguished from actual NASA measurements.

FLAMORA also offers Researcher Mode for detailed scientific exploration and Kids Mode, featuring simplified explanations, animations and guided learning.

Our goal is to make microgravity combustion research accessible, encourage scientific exploration and help identify knowledge gaps in fire safety for future space missions. Every result is distinguished as measured, derived or modelled to maintain scientific transparency.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

FLAMORA is a web platform that makes NASA's microgravity fire research searchable, comparable and easy to understand. It works in four layers:

1. Data: We downloaded the open experiment records and test tables for 23 combustion investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, including BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, Saffire and ACME. We cleaned them into 1,825 test records and 17,944 test conditions. Every cleaned value keeps its original value, unit and source file row. Suspect values are flagged, not deleted.

2. Database: The data is stored in a PostgreSQL database (Supabase) with search, links between experiments, materials, findings and sources, and security rules so the public can only read research data.

3. Analysis:

- Comparison engine: checks whether investigations can really be compared.

- Evidence ranking: shows which NASA tests are closest to the conditions of the ISS, a Moon base, a lunar rover or a Mars base, with the scoring criteria visible.

- Mission Brief: turns this into a one-page cited report for a chosen habitat.

4. AI assistant: a chatbot that searches our NASA database first and then writes an answer from that evidence only. Every answer cites its sources, and the server rejects any source the AI invents. If the data doesn't contain an answer, the assistant says so.

Users can also explore real flight data in charts, where clicking a point shows its source. A Fire Simulation lab lets them change gravity, oxygen, pressure and airflow to see how a flame changes, with the results always labelled "Modelled".

What benefits does it have?

- Saves time: findings spread across many datasets and papers are in one place, in comparable units.

- Honest comparisons: it explains when two experiments can't be compared (for example, a gas burner vs a solid sample), instead of mixing them.

- Shows the gaps: for example, NASA's PSI data has no solid materials tested at Moon-base air (30%+ oxygen at low pressure), and no fire tests at Moon or Mars gravity.

- Open to everyone: a Researcher mode for scientists and engineers, a Kids mode for students, and four languages (English, Mandarin, French, Hindi), with voice input.

What is the intended impact?

Future Moon bases and rovers will likely use air with more oxygen at lower pressure, which can make fires spread more easily. FLAMORA helps engineers and mission planners see quickly what NASA has already tested near those conditions and what still needs testing. It also helps students and the public understand why fire safety in space is hard, using real NASA results rather than guesses. More broadly, it shows how AI can make scientific data easier to use without inventing facts.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

- Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL, Python (data cleaning and checks).

- Frontend: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS.

- Backend and database: Next.js API routes, Supabase (PostgreSQL) with full-text search and row-level security.

- AI in the app: Google Gemini API (main) and Groq API (backup), behind a provider-independent layer.

- AI tools used to build it: Claude and Claude Code (research support, data checking, coding), Manus (first dataset build, then checked and corrected by our team), Google Stitch (UI designs).

- Testing: Vitest (117 automated tests) and production build checks.

- Data sources: NASA PSI open data (CC0), NASA Glenn fact sheets, NASA Technical Reports Server papers.

- Hardware: our own laptops. No special hardware.

How is the project creative?

- Every number has a label: Measured, Derived, Modelled, Illustrative or Not evaluated. Users always know whether they're looking at a real NASA measurement or a model.

- The AI is limited on purpose: it can only cite sources in our database. A made-up source is rejected, and "the data doesn't say" counts as a valid answer.

- Mission Brief: turns scattered research into a practical one-page report for a real future habitat, including what has never been tested.

- One dataset, two experiences: scientists and children see the same real numbers, explained at different levels.

- Simulation next to measurement: the model's prediction sits beside the nearest real NASA test, so users can see where the model is trustworthy and where it is only an estimate.

What factors did your team consider?

- Scientific accuracy:

- no invented data;

- suspect values and unit problems flagged openly;

- historical accidents (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir) never treated as experiments;

- Moon and Mars results always labelled as model estimates.

- Data quality: we found and fixed real problems in the raw data, including blank rows, typos such as "3400%" oxygen, mixed units and skipped columns, and we documented every fix.

- Accessibility:

- two reading levels;

- four languages, with the right fonts for Chinese and Hindi;

- voice input;

- keyboard navigation;

- mobile layouts.

- Privacy and security:

- API keys kept on the server;

- the public can only read research data;

- no personal data stored from the chat.

- Cost: free-tier AI and database services, so the project can stay online after the hackathon.

- Time: we built the most important features first, and clearly label anything unfinished as "Coming soon" instead of faking it.
